content: I called the Lantern's keeper and it wasn't the man in the corner who'd come for me — the keeper did, and now he was sliding a stool out from under the bar, nodding toward the back. "Fence is in the cellar. You're three minutes early, so you get the good table."

The Drowned Lantern swallows you in a hush of wet wool and spilled ale. The fire in the hearth fights a losing battle against the drizzle seeping through the panes, and the smell of brine and tallow hangs thick in the air.

Marro is in her usual corner, nursing a cup of something green. He has the look of a man who has seen better decades and worse men — a long nose, a face like crumpled parchment, and eyes that catalogue you before you've even sat down.

"Courier," he says, not quite a question. "You're dripping on my floorboards. Sit, or leave. But do it with your purse in mind either way."

Marro sits in the best chair, elbows on a scarred table, a clay pipe cold in his fingers. He has a scarred left eye and a smile that never quite reaches the good one. "Courier," he says, nodding at the wet shoulder-length auburn hair you carry like a curse. "Sit. You stink of harbor and trouble." He waves the innkeeper for two ales. "Now — the Gilded Gull. They moved their goods tonight, you say? Or is that what you *hope* I say?" He leans in, the bad eye sharp. "Words cost nothing out there. Proof costs. What have you got for me, Rook?" A framed notice hangs behind the bar where you'd expect a portrait — the harbor authority's daily log, ink still faintly tacky: :::card title="Harbor Notice — Drowned Lantern"

Office of the Harbourmaster

Night Tally · 14th of Mire

  • — Gull class Herald: LATE at berth
  • — Gull class Herald: cargo unaccounted
  • — Watch patrols doubled, Pier of Nails
  • — Informants: reward raised

— sealed in ink, Saltmere Harbour Authority —

:::

The Drowned Lantern smells of tar, cheap ale, and someone's fish dinner going off. A fisherman with a wooden hand is asleep in the corner. The barmaid, a girl with salt-streaked hair, eyes you but says nothing.

Marro is at the back, leaning against the barrels, peeling an orange with a short knife. He's a lean man with a scarred ear and a voice like gravel in a tin can. "Rook. You look like the harbor itself." He peels off a segment of orange and pops it in his mouth. "What do you want, courier? News, trouble, or a job?"

I can see Marro's eyes flick to the sealed satchel, then back to your face. He slides a coin purse across the wet table. "Fifty," he amends. "Rain, Rook. Bad night for a man to walk the docks. You've earned the extra."

The Drowned Lantern smells of salt, wet wool, and cheap gin. A handful of dockers hunch at the bar, their breath fogging in the low amber light, but it's the back corner where the air turns quiet — a thickset man with a crooked nose and a sleeve of tattooed eels peels an orange with the casual menace of a man who expects to be paid for the peel.

Marro looks up. "You," he says, as though you owe him a favor. "I said no jobs north of the Mole until the watch cooled off, and they're not cooling off. Three of our boys got walked this week. So unless you've got silver for news, you're wasting my lamp oil."

He finishes the peel in one long spiral and drops it in the glass between you. "What did the Lighthouse take to make you brave enough to walk in here?"

:::card title="The Drowned Lantern — back booth"
The Drowned Lantern

"Courier's fare. Sealed goods, sealed mouths. Forty gold, no questions asked." — scratched into the booth's arm, generations deep.

::: Marro's ledger-craze softens when his fingers brush the satchel. He turns it once, thumbing the wax seal with a professional respect. "Sealed goods, sealed mouths." He nods slowly, and a boy in a corner begins moving toward the back room with a string of coins. "You're in for a while, then. What's the name on the seal?"

Marro's eyes slide from your face to the satchel, and something in his posture tightens — a fence notices when a courier shows up with sealed work.

"Forty," he repeats, tasting the number. "And for *what* exactly did you risk the rain for, friend?" He taps the table once, deliberately. "I'll pay the moment I know it's worth my coin. Sealed parcels don't talk, but men do."

:::card title="The Drowned Lantern"
🏮
THE DROWNED LANTERN
"Where salt meets shadow"
— — — — — — — — —
Harbor District Est. 1741
No watchmen. No questions.
For now.
::: Marro doesn't move his hand from his cups. His eyes travel over the satchel like a man measuring a body. He pushes back a strand of hair from his forehead, and it sticks — damp, or thin, or both. "Sealed?" he murmurs, tilting his head. "You don't open it, right?" A pause, and something almost like fear in his voice, which is strange for a fence. "Forty's fine. I've got it in the drawer." He slides a cloth-wrapped stack across the scarred table — you don't need to count to know it's right. "Who's the sender?" he asks, leaning forward. "Just. For the file."

Marro's eyes go to the satchel before they come to your face. He leans in, voice dropping under the creak of the tap.

"Forty is for *delivered*, Rook, not for *shown*. What's inside?"
I'm a game master, not the player character. I'll narrate the scene but I can't control Rook's choices—those are yours to make. Let me set the moment.

Marro's eyes flick to the satchel before he even answers. "Like we agreed," he repeats, and there's a smile in it that doesn't reach anything. "And before you think it — I'm not shorting you. I'm *testing* you."

He produces a pouch from under the table, tips a cascade of coins across the scarred wood. They clatter like teeth. "Seal's unbroken, I can't argue with that. Question is whether the man inside this port's guard-house will argue with *you*."

He leans in, voice dropping. "Saltmere Watch has been sniffing around the shipping ledgers all week. Word is they're looking for a courier who moves the wrong cargo. That satchel you just set on my table — do you know what's in it?"

:::choices
- "You told me not to ask."
- "I don't. I'm a courier, not a goddamn customs officer."
- "What are you really asking?"
- [Write your own]
:::

Marro leans in, ink-stained fingers tapping the table. 'Last seen on the quays, third mooring from the customs house. A man in a salt-grey coat hauled it across the rail just before your rain kicked in. Watch was still out on patrol — if you're going to lift it from him, do it quick and quiet, or the whole quarter will be ringing by the time you've reached the stairs.'

Marro slides a tankard of amber ale across the scarred wood before you've even sat back, then spreads his ink-stained fingers on the table like he's about to deal cards.

"Forty gold for a sealed satchel that hasn't opened yet," he says, voice low and careful. "You know how this works, Rook. I pay when the seal's off and I know what's inside." He taps the leather. "The man who gave you this? He paid me. I'm the one still waiting."

He leans in, and the taproom noise — rain on the window, a cough from the bar — seems to hush around the booth. "Give me the seal. I'll be generous."

Marro's fingers drum the table — one coin, then two, testing their weight before he slides it back toward you. His eyes flick to the satchel, then to the door, then back.

"Forty gold's what we agreed *for the run*," he murmurs, low enough that the tallow smoke does the rest of his silencing. "The satchel's still sealed, Rook. Sealed means the harbor master's mark's on it, and harbor master's mark means his men might be asking questions at the watergate." He leans in. "You got a buyer, or are we still guessing?"

Rain still ticks off the roof outside.

:::card title="The Drowned Lantern — Ledger"
SALTWERE COURIER — LEDGER
F. Mares40 g
——
sealed · unsigned
::: Marro's thumb flicks the satchel's seal, eyes never leaving your face. "Sealed thing. I don't ask what's inside, courier's privilege — but I *do* ask why a man's paying forty gold to move a package no one's named a drop point for." He pushes a small leather pouch across the scarred wood. It clinks honest. "Here. Tell me the drop and I'll name a man who delivers blind."

The Drowned Lantern's door bangs open — a watch-sergeant, rain dripping from a steel cap, scanning the room. 'No fresh faces, no business done. By order of the harbormaster.' Marro's coin purse freezes halfway to your belt.

Marro taps a map spread on the table, a fingertip tracing the harbor line. 'Last night, dockside. Some say it was a water thief off the Pelican. Others say a clerk's shadow slipped out the harbor office with it tucked under his arm.' He leans in. 'Dawn, Rook. The watch is already thick on the quay — and they'll be thicker by morning.'

Marro leans back, steepling his ink-black fingers. 'Last seen by a watch-sweeper on Brine Row. He'd say the ledger's moving through the old fish market by now — somewhere under the wharf, where the light don't reach and the tide keeps its own hours.'

He taps the table where the satchel still lies. 'Watchmen've got the market locked down since the theft. You walk in plain, you'll be a body by noon.'

Marro leans close, voice dropping to a rasp. 'Last seen in the Custom House vault — that's a bad place for a courier to go alone. Or... it's in the hands of a woman called Sera Voss. She trades in stolen records from the docks. She's seen at the Gilded Anchor tavern most nights.' He taps the table. 'Your call, Rook. Vault or Voss. And you'd best not linger, either way. The watch has been prowling the harbor like starved dogs since the theft.'

'Last seen crossing the Tidal Yards with a salt-merchant's seal on the cover,' Marro says, tapping the table. 'Watch out — the harbor wardens are on red alert since the theft. Two patrols a night, lanterns swinging wide.'

He drops a folded paper on the table. 'Buy a night on the fishwife's gallery above the chandler's row — she doesn't ask why you're watching.'

Marro taps the table with a stained finger. 'The wharf office on Gull Street. Last seen with Aldric's runner, two watches before the tide turned.' He slides a folded slip of paper across the boards. 'Aldric's seal on the door. You go in quiet, you come out with the ledger. Anything loud, and the watch is on you before you can blink.'

Marro draws a slow finger over the board, leaving a dark track. 'Harbormaster Vane keeps it in the salt house by the crane yards. Guarded, so. And word is the watch has been circling since it vanished — Vane's got every bell in the city rung.' He taps the ledger's spot on his map. 'Go in the tide, Rook. Or don't go in at all — but the purse don't grow back.'

Marro leans in, lowering his voice beneath the tap's noise. 'The Salt Archive, two streets up. Watch took over the lock last night — the old clerk, Hest, swore he saw the thief slip out the harbor side. That's your window.' He taps the table once. 'Bring me the ledger, Rook. Not a copy. The whole book.'

The map's lines run close together now — Rat Alley is a throat of a street wedged between the chandlery's oil-stained wall and a fish market's rotting stalls. Rain runs off the awnings in steady sheets.

Halfway down, a light flickers from a doorway: an oil lamp swaying on a nail, and its silhouette — broad-shouldered, one eye catching the glow like a cat's.

"Got company," says a voice that sounds like gravel dragged over rope. "Or got trouble. Either way, I'm bored."

Marro leans in, voice dropping to a rasp. 'Last seen in the hands of Warden Corvain at the Customs House — or rather, taken from there. He's been guarding it in his office like a man with something to hide.' He taps the table, ink smearing a ring of varnish. 'Door's barred by dawn lock. Watch is thick that time — three on the beat and a lantern-lady circling. If you want it without bells, go dark and be fast.' He shrugs, as if the watch isn't his problem. :::card title="The Drowned Lantern — Booth Notes"
Job Slip
Objective: Recover the harbormaster's ledger
Last seen: Warden Corvain's office, Customs House
Deadline: By dawn
Note: Dawn-locked door · 3 watch on beat · lantern-lady circling
Pay on return: TBD
::: The rain hammers the shingles overhead. Marro is already counting a new coin, his eyes drifting away from you — he's decided, or he's deciding, whether you're the one who gets this job done or the one they find in the water.

The alley squats between the chandlery's sagging warehouse and a wall slick with black algae. Somewhere below, Gessa is sleeping it off or waiting it out — one-eyed thugs always pick one.

The rain has eased to a mist, but the street's slick, and the only dry cover is under the chandlery's eaves, where coils of rope and a single unlit lantern make poor company.
Rain slicks the cobblestones of Rat Alley, turning the garbage into a black mirror. The chandlery's back door hangs off its hinges, a gap of darkness where Gessa keeps her stolen goods.

The cudgel crackles past your ear, and you roll, feeling a hot stitch in your bruised ribs. You come up with the blade out, but Gessa is already there, swinging again with the strength of a dockworker who's hauled cable for twenty years.

The map Marro pressed into your hands is already spotted with rain. Rat Alley is a gullet of slick stone between the chandlery and a dead fish market, and the stink of brine is enough to coat the back of your throat.

You find the chandlery's back door, chained shut. Around the corner, behind a stack of rotting barrels, a single lantern swings. A woman leans against the wall beside it — broad shoulders, a scar splitting her left eyebrow, and indeed only one eye, though you can't tell which one is the good one. She's been watching the alley mouth. She's been watching you.

The cudgel cracks against your ribs and the air leaves your lungs in a gasp. You bring the shortsword up just in time to take her second swing — the flat of the blade bites into the wood of the cudgel with a sharp crack. Gessa's good eye widens. "You've got a knife, then, ratling." She kicks out — her boot finds your knee and you fold.
I'll weave the rib blow into Rook's battered state and log the encounter.

Gessa's cudgel carves the air again. You drop low as it cracks the barrel behind you, and your shortsword slides into her thigh with a dull thud. She snarls, grabs the blade, and wrenches you close.

You put your shoulder into her gut and drive the pommel into her jaw. She staggers, the cudgel clattering to the wet cobble. There's a satchel at her hip, straps still wet from the rain.

Gessa's cudgel cracks across your ribs and the world tilts sideways — a hot stitch of pain under your arm. You draw, and the one-eyed woman snarls, swinging wide again, the cudgel whistling through the rain.

"Harbormaster's books? You got the wrong alley, courier."

You're breathing hard, the rain running through the gap where her swing found you.

The cudgel bites and you stagger, ribs screaming. But you draw the shortsword clean, and the alley tightens around the two of you.

Gessa grins through a gap of yellow teeth. "Courier, eh? Gotta be worth a kill if Marro pays for you. Give me the ledger, give me the purse, or I'll crack that blade off your fingers."

She shifts her weight, cudgel back, ready to come in again.

The cudgel comes down again, cracking off your blade with a sound like a dropped plate. Gessa roars and swings low, but you're already stepping off the center line, the rain hissing as your shortsword finds the gap beneath her ribs. She doubles over, cursing, and the alley lights flicker.

The cudgel cracks down on your shoulder before you clear your stance. You roll with it, tasting blood, and the shortsword hisses out — but Gessa's one bad eye still sees you coming. She swings again, wilder now, and you slide beneath the arc, feeling the wind of it brush your hair.

Your blade opens a shallow line on her forearm; she snarls, drops her shoulder, and rams you both feet running into the mud.

The alley is empty save for the two of you, but the rain hides nothing from the watch if one of you shouts it.

Blood beads at the wound, and Gessa sinks to her knees, clutching her thigh. She spits at your boots. "Harbormaster's office will know that book's missing. You've got maybe two hours before the watch goes door to door."

Your ribs still burn. The rain keeps falling on you both, and the alley is empty except for the swinging lantern and your own breath.

The cudgel crashes down again, and this time you block on the flat of your blade, sparks jumping off the wet cobblestones. Your ribs throb with every breath — the first blow is still a knot of fire in your side.

Gessa is faster than she looks, but she's only one hand in the fight; the other grips a rusted hook she uses to catch your wrist and yank you off-balance.

You're breathing hard now, and the alley's black and close, and every swing costs you more than it should.

Blood wells from the cut across her thigh and Gessa's hand finds it, her grin gone. She's still up, still circling, but slow now — rain running dark down the cobbles around her boots.

"Got the ledger," you say, keeping the sword low and the distance honest. "Walk away. This isn't worth a fight you can't win."

Behind you, a lantern swings and clatters. The alley mouth narrows. You've got the book — but you're cut, tired, and the watch might come looking for a thief with a fresh cut across their thigh before the dawn deadline Marro set.

The cut opens clean and Gessa hisses through her teeth, dropping to one knee in the rain. Blood and gutter-water run together down her leg. She glares up at you, the ledger still clutched to her chest.

"Talk," she wheezes. "I'll talk anything you want. Just—"

The ledger is the one from the harbormaster's office, its clasp dented but sealed. You can drag it to Marro before dawn, or press Gessa for more while she's still able to rattle off names.

Gessa crumples against the chandlery wall, cradling her thigh. "Take it, courier. But the watch is coming—there's a whistle on the quay tonight." She spits blood onto the wet stones.

You grab the ledger, still warm from her coat.

Gessa crumples against the wall, one hand clamped to the cut above her knee. "Fine, fine! I've more sense than blood."

She's still breathing hard when she nods toward a rusted grate set low in the chandlery wall. "The ledger came through there, last night. I'm paid to watch the alley, not to win fights. Take your book and be gone."

You tuck the ledger inside your drenched cloak. The rain hasn't let up, and your ribs still ache every time you shift.

Gessa yowls and sinks into the dark, clutching her thigh. The leather-bound ledger lies in a puddle at your feet, rain-darkened and heavy.

You're breathing hard, and the cut along your ribs aches with every gust of wind through the alley. Behind Gessa, a lantern swings in the rain — she's running toward it, calling for a watchmate.

The ledger is warm in your hand and Gessa is down, pressing a rag to her thigh, hissing through her teeth. 'The watch rounds this alley in the hour,' she spits. 'And now they'll have my name. Make it hurt.'

Rain drums on the barrel-staves overhead. Somewhere a harbor bell begins to toll the third watch.

Gessa crumples to one knee, the cudgel clattering away into the dark. She grabs her thigh and hisses through her teeth — the rain runs red over her boots before the black water takes it.

The ledger's there on the stones, dripping. She doesn't look up as you pass. 'The harbormaster'll want it back,' she wheezes. 'But not the way you think. Read the last page before you hand it over, courier.'

Gessa goes down hard on the wet cobbles, clutching her thigh. Blood streaks the water running past her ankle. She glares up at you through the rain.

'Next time,' she hisses, 'I'm telling the watch. Mark me, courier — I remember faces.'

The ledger lies where it fell, black leather weeping rain. You've got it. The question is what Gessa's grudge is worth, and how long before the harbor watch starts asking questions.

The cut opens red and Gessa staggers, one hand clamping her thigh as she backs toward the chandlery wall. Her eye goes wide, darting down the alley, hunting a way out before she's gone.

"Easy now," you hear yourself say, sword still low. "Just the ledger."

Rain hammers the gut. Somewhere beyond the lean-to shadows a dog barks, then stops.

The linen's tight, but the ribs still protest with every step. You duck out of Rat Alley and into the wider lane, the ledger heavy against your hip.

A block over, a watch-lantern swings from a bracket — a pair of wardens on beat, not yet close. The Drowned Lantern's sign bobs ahead, wet and yellow.

"Race you," you mutter to no one, and pick up the pace.

The leather binding soaks up rain as you go. Your breath comes in short, sharp pulls against the bandage, each step a small negotiation between pain and momentum. Rat Alley opens back onto the harbor road, and beyond it Saltmere is waking — gulls screaming, halyards clattering in the wind, and far off, the bells of the Tide Temple striking the hour.

Dawn is still two hours off, but the watch will be out in two more. You've got the ledger, you've got your purse, and you've got ribs that throb like a second heartbeat.

The ledger is heavier than it looks — brass clasp warm from Gessa's coat. You duck into a drainage cut as a watch bell tolls from the harbor, and for a moment the whole alley seems to hold its breath.

By the time you crest the far rise, Rain's Mouth has opened into the wet square where the Drowned Lantern waits, its yellow light a soft wound in the dark.

The linen is a tight bandage, not a fix. Every breath now pulls at the bruised flesh, and the alley's cold seeps in through the wet cloak.

Behind you, Gessa's cries echo off the warehouses as she staggers deeper into Rat Alley. The only sound now is rain and your own ragged breathing. Dawn will come, and the harbormaster's desk is that way — past the Customs Arch. You can almost feel the heat of your ribs with each step.

The path out of Rat Alley lies through the cobbles of Lantern Row, where the streetlamps are already being lit. Saltmere's watch patrols the arch in pairs. One wrong move and the whole city will know your face by morning.

The fish market is a river of wet slick and brine. You go low, ducking under a hanging lamp and under the swinging knife of a gutting stall. The bells hammer your bruised ribs with every stride.

By the time you reach the watergate, your lungs are a furnace and the world edges in. You slide through the grate in the sea wall, the cold stinging the cut in your side, and surface in the black water on the far side.

You have the ledger. Dawn is hours off. The question now is how to get back to Marro's without a second whistle finding you.

The alley exhales as you move. By the time you've cleared the chandlery wall, Gessa's howl has faded to a whimper and no watch whistle answers it — the city's eye on you barely a glint.

But your ribs are another story. The linen bandage holds, yet every breath is a small negotiation, and your legs are burning from the fight you barely won. You've got a ledger to deliver and a dawn to make, with the rain still working the stones slick.
The harbormaster takes the ledger without looking up, checking the seal. 'Clean work, Rook. That's thirty gold, and a favor I'll remember.' He presses the coin purse into your hand.

The harbormaster's grip is a vise as he snatches the ledger. His eyes go wide over its pages. 'Midnight. You beat the watch to me.' He shoves a small silver coin into your palm — more than Marro promised, though Marro won't see it.

Below, boots on stone and the clash of watch-bells. The alarm is out now, and the tower door will be found.

You have one way down: the window, forty feet to the wet cobbles of the harbor lane.

The harbormaster's lantern-light spilling across the ledger confirms it — the clasp still shut, the ink dark. He presses a coin into your palm, heavier than it looks, and his eye drops toward the stairs as the whistle carries up from the fish market below. 'Quickly, then. There's a way down I'd rather you used than climbed up.'

Marro will want to hear that it's done, and there's still rain left in the night to run through.

The harbormaster's hand is cold and shaking. He takes the ledger, holds it to the lantern light, and lets out a breath that sounds almost like a sob.

"That'll be ten gold," he says, pressing coins into your palm, "and if you ever tell the watch who turned it in... I owe you a debt that never dies."

The bells have stopped. Through the window, the rain keeps falling, and somewhere below, the city goes on breathing.

The harbormaster takes the ledger with both hands, his eyes going bright as he checks the clasp. He counts out the promised forty gold in old, heavy pieces — the same as Marro, no less.

"You came through the fish market?" he murmurs, frowning toward the window as if he can see the whistle still shrilling. "That line is watched. Word will be on you by morning."

He tucks the coin into your grip and slips a brass token into your other hand — a harbormaster's mark, good for safe passage in any of his houses.

The harbormaster, a thick-set woman in a damp oilskin coat, takes the ledger in one hand and examines the clasp with the other. Her face stays unreadable until she turns to a ledger room door.

'You were here after midnight, fighting in Rat Alley, and the bells are still ringing. That's a lot of witnesses.' She slides a small pouch of coin across the counter — lighter than Marro's purse. 'Thirty, not forty. And get out of my tower before I call the watch to confirm what you did.'

Outside, the whistle Gessa screamed has drawn a patrol; lanterns cut through the rain at the harbor mouth, moving your way.

The rain has turned the cobbles to black glass. Behind you the watch bells have quieted, but you can still feel the city holding its breath.

You push through the Drowned Lantern's door. Marro is still in his booth, but the lantern light seems thinner. His eyes go to your bandaged ribs, then to your pack.

'You walked all that with those ribs?' A dry grin. He slides a second purse across the boards. 'Harbormaster's cut. She mentioned your name.'

:::choices
- Take the purse and drink
- Ask Marro for more work
- Head for a room before the rain worsens
:::

The harbormaster's eyes go flat, then quick. 'Inside. Now.' He takes the ledger before it can sink further, snuffing the candle with a breath that smells of pipe ash.

'You're lucky I keep the door unlocked for you,' he mutters, already working the clasp. 'Word of the theft gets to the watch by dawn. That means you owe Marro twice as much for bringing it home, and twice as little for living to collect.'

Outside the window, lanterns and boots on wet stone: two watchmen cross the yard toward the tower stairs.

The rain is easing to a drizzle as you cross the quay. The Drowned Lantern's lamp still burns green above the street.

Marro is waiting in the same booth, but he's not alone — a watch sergeant in grey stands at his elbow, hand on his sword. He looks you up and down, and the room goes quiet.

The tower stair door bangs shut behind you, and the rain closes over your head again. Your ribs ache with every stride; the signet ring sits cold in your fist. The Drowned Lantern's glow should be two blocks north.

A figure in a watchman's livery rounds the corner ahead, lantern swinging, scanning the alley. The heat is on, and it's coming this way.

The door swings on a groan. The harbormaster — a thick woman with salt-white hair — takes the ledger, checks the clasp, then looks you up and down, eyes stopping on your linen bandage.

'That'll be a story for later,' she says, pressing two gold pieces into your palm. 'You've made a friend tonight, courier.'

The harbormaster takes the ledger without a word, his wet gloves black to the knuckles. He flips the brass clasp open, checks a page, and closes it again. Then he presses a folded note into your palm and slips back inside. The door swings shut behind him. Outside, the watch lanterns are converging on the tower — and the note in your hand isn't payment. :::card title="Harbormaster's Note"

Rook,

You brought the ledger. That buys you my silence tonight.

Meet me at the Dry Docks, the third mooring, before the tide turns. Bring your ears, not your sword.

— V.

no seal · no date

:::

The stairwell door slams behind you and the rain greets you like an old enemy. Your bound ribs throb with every wet breath as you angle back down the seawall toward the lantern's amber glow.

You push through the Drowned Lantern's door and straight into Marro's booth. He's been waiting — and he's not alone. Two figures flank him in the shadows, faces half-hidden under hoods. One of them, a broad-shouldered woman with a shaved head, is watching your pack with open, hungry interest.

Marro smiles without warmth. 'Good work, Rook. Now the question is — does the ledger go to the harbormaster, or does it go to *us*?'

The stairs creak behind you as you descend, the signet ring cold in your pocket. By the time you reach the harbor lane the rain has eased to a drizzle, and the Drowned Lantern's amber glow is still spilling across the cobbles like spilled tea.

Marro is gone. His empty chair is still pushed back, and a chalk tally remains on the bar — but the back room door hangs open and no one answers your knock. The only one left in the taproom is the quiet woman by the hearth, watching you with steady eyes.

"Marro?" you ask.

She shrugs toward the door. "Left an hour past, heading toward the north docks. Said something about 'a delivery that wouldn't wait for the bells.'" She pauses. "Didn't look like a man in a hurry to be found."

The Drowned Lantern's door swings open to the same tallow smell. Marro is still in the back booth, but his ink-stained fingers have gone still, and his eyes flick to the door.

'You have the watch breathing down your neck,' he says quietly, pushing a second purse across the boards. 'And a man with a silver ring is asking about you. So — you want to walk into the light, or do we find you a roof for the night?'

You pocket the silver ring. The rain has eased to a drizzle by the time you reach the Drowned Lantern, though the night still smells of salt and tar.

Marro is waiting in his booth, a stub of pipe glowing between his teeth. He glances at your bruised ribs, then at the empty space where the ledger was. 'Word travels fast in the harbor.' He slides a coin purse across the boards—this one heavier than the first.

'One more thing, Rook. You've earned it. There's a crate of "special" imports locked in the vault at the old warehouse district. My man says the lock is a simple thing. If you can crack it, the contents are yours.'

The tower door swings shut behind you, sealing in the lantern glow. Out, the rain has turned to a cold hiss off the wet cobbles. Every breath still bites through the linen band across your ribs.

You duck the corner toward the Drowned Lantern, cutting through the fish market's emptying stalls. The watch whistle is quieter now — just a distant moan over the water.

The rain has eased to a drizzle by the time you reach the Drowned Lantern. Marro is where he left you — back booth, ink-stained fingers tapping the table. He eyes your bound ribs and the ledger still in your pack.

"Well, well. Didn't take you all night." He slides a second purse across the boards. "Fifty for the ledger. And you still owe me that favor."

The taproom is half-full tonight — sailors, a couple of dockworkers, and a hooded figure in the corner who watches you with particular interest as you approach the booth.

The rain has turned to a fine mist as you cross back through the market. The Drowned Lantern glows warm through the dark. Marro is at the same booth, nursing a cup, waiting for the ledger's return.

'Gessa let it go easy,' he says, eyes flicking over your ribs before he can catch himself. 'Silver ring, I take it.'
